newsitem.title: UK: British insurance fraud falls for fourth year.
newsitem.headline: British insurance fraud falls for fourth year.

text.p: Fraudulent insurance claims fell for the fourth year running in Britain in 1996, according to the latest survey by the Association of British Insurers (ABI).
The estimated cost of false claims in the past year of 560 million pounds ($928 million), is down 4.5 percent on 1995.
The results of the survey coincide with the Association's Annual Fraud Seminar in London on Thursday which will discuss the latest moves to counter fraud.

Among those caught out in the past year was a man who claimed 14,000 pounds for medical treatment and convalesence in Africa following a bout of malaria. The hospital' turned out to be a local brothel.
Another man who claimed medical costs for an operation to remove his appendix was discovered to have claimed for the removal of the same appendix previously - 17 times.

Inflated claims remain the most common type of fraud, making up nearly two-fifths of the total cost to the industry. Next comes misrepresentation -- providing misleading information, for example about claims made in the past -- which accounts for nearly one third.
Both motor and household insurance fraud fell in 1996 though fraudulent claims under creditor and personal accident policies increased slightly.

"It is very encouraging that the estimated cost of fraudulent insurance claims has fallen for the fourth year running. But the 560 million pound total does, however, remain too high and we are determined to reduce it," said Mark Boleat, ABI's Director General.
Boleat said there was evidence of fraud cases involving more than one country and that this must be the next priority for the industry.
